question: A shared services director says the invoice-processing team should be "more efficient" and asks an analyst to use Claude to work out how. What should the analyst do first?
options: A) Ask Claude to list the common inefficiencies in invoice processing and check which of them apply here.
B) Ask the invoice team which parts of their work they would most like to stop doing altogether now.
C) Agree with the director which measure of efficiency matters: cycle time, cost per invoice, or errors.
D) Ask Claude to redesign the invoice process end to end so the director can see what is possible.
correct_answers: C) Agree with the director which measure of efficiency matters: cycle time, cost per invoice, or errors.
explanations: A generic list of inefficiencies gives the analyst somewhere to look but no way to prioritise. Whether a given inefficiency is worth removing depends on which measure the director cares about, which has not been settled.

The team's least favourite tasks are worth hearing and may be a good source of hypotheses, but they indicate irritation rather than cost. The analyst would still not know which measure of efficiency the director wants moved.

Correct. Efficiency pulls in different directions: faster processing can raise error rates, and cutting cost per invoice can lengthen cycle time. Fixing which measure matters turns a vague instruction into a target the analysis can aim at and later be judged against.

A full redesign produced before the goal is agreed optimises for whatever the tool assumes efficiency means. It also invites the director to react to a finished proposal rather than to state the outcome being sought.
